patterns.name: comment.block.carve
patterns.comment: A %%% fence line is a delimiter plus an insignificant tail (spec PART 9 section 28): only the leading run of % is structural, so `%%% TODO` opens and `%%% end` closes. %%% carries no info string - a raw passthrough block is a CODE fence with an =FORMAT info string - so `%%% html` is a comment. The end backreference matches the opener width exactly, so %%%% nests %%%.

patterns.name: markup.other.figure-group.carve
patterns.comment: COMPOSITE FIGURE (PART 9 S4c, markup-carve/carve#1215; ported from markup-carve/carve-grammars#223, tracked by markup-carve/carve-grammars#222). The kind word `figure` is reserved among the `:::` types: a BARE opener - the fence, its separator, the word `figure`, and NOTHING else - is ONE figure of ordered panels, not an admonition, so it carries its own scope and this pattern sits BEFORE the generic div pattern below. THE WHOLE DISTINCTION IS THE TAIL of one line: an opener carrying a quoted title or a `[label]` (`::: figure "T"`, `::: figure [g]`) is not that production at all, does not match here, and falls through to the div pattern - which is the generic Tier-2 container the clause says it stays, with title and label preserved. THE SEPARATOR IS A SPACE RUN, NEVER A TAB (grammar.ebnf PART 7, MARKER SEPARATORS; corpus 254): `:::<TAB>figure` renders as a paragraph, so it is spelled ` +` rather than the `\s*` the div pattern beside it uses - a tab-separated opener falls to that pattern and reads exactly as it does today, an over-colouring this rule neither widens nor fixes. Trailing whitespace after the kind word is insignificant and may be a tab. THE GROUP CAPTION NEEDS NO RULE: it is an ordinary `^ ` line one line below the closing fence, which the caption pattern under `#tables` already claims at document level and inside every container body. The optional bullet prefix is carried over from the div pattern, because a group may open directly after a list marker (`- ::: figure`) just as an admonition may. RESIDUAL, written down rather than left to be rediscovered: GROUPS DO NOT NEST - a bare `::: figure` at any depth inside an open group is a generic container - but a `:::` opener here is a per-line `match` with no region, so this grammar has no notion of being inside one and over-colours the inner opener as a group too. carve-grammars carries that rule through a begin/end pair; restructuring the div pattern into begin/end is what it would take here as well, and is deliberately not part of this change.

patterns.name: markup.other.div.carve
patterns.comment: A div fence may open directly after a list marker (`- ::: note`), so an optional bullet prefix is consumed here and scoped as a list marker. A BARE `::: figure` opener never reaches this pattern: it is a composite figure, not a generic container, and the pattern above claims it first (PART 9 S4c). An opener carrying a title or a `[label]` does reach it, which is the point of the split.

GFM delimiter/alignment row: a whole line of only pipes, dashes, optional alignment colons, and whitespace (e.g. `|---|---|`, `|:---:|`). Gated by a full-row lookahead so an ordinary data cell that merely contains dashes is NOT mis-scoped. Each dash/colon cell is the separator; the pipes keep their separator scope. Note: TextMate rules are line-local and do not track table position, so a dash/colon-only row that is NOT the parser's second-row delimiter (e.g. a body row that happens to be all dashes) is also highlighted here. That edge case is rare and cosmetic; modeling exact delimiter-row position would require a full multi-line table state machine.
patterns.name: markup.table.row.separator.carve

patterns.comment: Separator cell: leading/trailing alignment colons get a dedicated alignment scope; the dash run stays the separator punctuation.
A lone `+` at the marker column is the list-continuation marker, not a bullet (`+` is never a bullet in Carve).
patterns.name: markup.list.continuation.carve

patterns.comment: A LIST ITEM IS A CONTAINER, NOT A LINE (markup-carve/vscode-carve#61, ported from markup-carve/carve-grammars#94). It opens on its marker line, stays open across blank lines, and closes on the first nonblank line indented BELOW its content column - the marker's ACTUAL width, `indent + marker + separator`, not a fixed two columns. That is what tells an indented definition apart from a below-column one: `- a` over `  [r]: /u` keeps its definition, while `- - a` over ` [^f]: x` sits below every open content column and is item TEXT that defines nothing (corpus a-definition-below-every-content-column-folds-as-text, markup-carve/carve#624). A TASK ITEM'S CONTENT COLUMN IS TWO PAST THE INDENT WHATEVER THE SEPARATOR IS - the checkbox absorbs the rest, so it gets its own branch ahead of the plain bullet rather than inheriting the marker-width test. Measured, not assumed: carve-php and carve-js agree that a body line two columns in belongs to the item for every separator width from one space to five, where the same widths under a plain bullet carry the column with them (`-   a` puts its body at column 4, `-   [x] a` keeps it at column 2). The checkbox glued to an attribute block (`-{.c} [x] done`) is still not scoped - the known limitation this branch inherits, not one it adds.

A LIST ITEM IS A CONTAINER, NOT A LINE (markup-carve/vscode-carve#61, ported from markup-carve/carve-grammars#94). It opens on its marker line, stays open across blank lines, and closes on the first nonblank line indented BELOW its content column - the marker's ACTUAL width, `indent + marker + separator`, not a fixed two columns. That is what tells an indented definition apart from a below-column one: `- a` over `  [r]: /u` keeps its definition, while `- - a` over ` [^f]: x` sits below every open content column and is item TEXT that defines nothing (corpus a-definition-below-every-content-column-folds-as-text, markup-carve/carve#624). THE TEST IS EXACT FOR A BULLET at any indent and any separator width: a bullet marker is one column and the separator is captured whitespace, so `\1[ \t]\3` reconstructs the column count from the marker line itself. A TAB counts as one column here rather than advancing to the next tab stop, and a continuation line has to repeat the marker line's own indent characters. A marker line may carry several markers (`- - A` opens two nested lists), so scope each one, not only the line-anchored first. A BULLET MAY BE GLUED TO AN ATTRIBUTE BLOCK, and then the required space comes after the block, not after the marker - so `-{#x} item` and `*{.c} item` went uncoloured on a line that IS a list item, while the ordered rule beside it already had the branch (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126). It is a LOOKAHEAD: consuming the block would make this rule own those characters, so the attribute rule could no longer scope them. KNOWN LIMITATION, shared with every Carve TextMate grammar: the checkbox after a glued block (`-{.c} [x] done`) is not scoped, because the task branch has none; the bullet is. THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126).

The attribute-glued bullet (`-{#x} item`). Its content column cannot be counted, because the block's width is not whitespace, so this branch uses the MINIMUM content column, indent plus two: the container stays open across a range an exact test would have closed, which is the over-coloring side every block rule in this grammar already takes. A marker line may carry several markers (`- - A` opens two nested lists), so scope each one, not only the line-anchored first. A BULLET MAY BE GLUED TO AN ATTRIBUTE BLOCK, and then the required space comes after the block, not after the marker - so `-{#x} item` and `*{.c} item` went uncoloured on a line that IS a list item, while the ordered rule beside it already had the branch (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126). It is a LOOKAHEAD: consuming the block would make this rule own those characters, so the attribute rule could no longer scope them. KNOWN LIMITATION, shared with every Carve TextMate grammar: the checkbox after a glued block (`-{.c} [x] done`) is not scoped, because the task branch has none; the bullet is. THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126).

A LIST ITEM IS A CONTAINER, NOT A LINE (markup-carve/vscode-carve#61, ported from markup-carve/carve-grammars#94). It opens on its marker line, stays open across blank lines, and closes on the first nonblank line indented BELOW its content column - the marker's ACTUAL width, `indent + marker + separator`, not a fixed two columns. That is what tells an indented definition apart from a below-column one: `- a` over `  [r]: /u` keeps its definition, while `- - a` over ` [^f]: x` sits below every open content column and is item TEXT that defines nothing (corpus a-definition-below-every-content-column-folds-as-text, markup-carve/carve#624). AN ORDERED MARKER IS NOT ONE COLUMN WIDE, and Oniguruma cannot count the width of a captured run - vscode-textmate splices a begin capture into the `end` pattern as literal TEXT, so a backreference reproduces the marker's characters, never its length. The width is therefore spelled out: one branch per marker width, each consuming exactly that many characters and asking its `end` for exactly that many columns. EXACT for widths 1 to 5 (`.`, `1.`, `10.`, `iii.`, `1000.`), which covers every ordered marker in the corpus; the width-5 branch also accepts anything wider and under-counts it, holding the container open a column or two too long rather than closing it early. Ordered markers use a trailing `.` or `)` only. A parenthesized `(1)` / `(a)` form is NOT a marker in Carve (it is too easily confused with prose), so no leading `(`. The BARE DOT is a marker on its own (carve#472): `.` continues an ordered sequence, and is the only marker allowed to drop its value. The lookahead admits a marker glued to an attribute block (`.{#x}`, `3.{#k v}`), which is how the corpus writes it - but the ATTRIBUTE FORM NEEDS CONTENT TOO: `1.{#x}` with nothing after the block is a paragraph, so the glued-block branch spells the block out in full rather than skipping it. A `\{[^}]*\}` run stops in the wrong place, because a quoted value may contain `}` and may escape its own quote, and `{title="a}b"} x` is a valid item (markup-carve/carve-grammars#85). A ROMAN RUN IS CASE-CONSISTENT: two classes, not one `[ivxlcdmIVXLCDM]`, which matched any mixture and coloured `Vim. text` and `Mix. text` as lists where carve-js renders paragraphs (markup-carve/carve-grammars#118). `mix.`, `civil.` and `did.` DO open lists, so the fix is the case split rather than rejecting multi-letter words. THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126).
Ordered marker, width 2. See the width-1 branch above for why the widths are spelled out one branch at a time.
Ordered marker, width 3. See the width-1 branch above for why the widths are spelled out one branch at a time.
Ordered marker, width 4. See the width-1 branch above for why the widths are spelled out one branch at a time.
Ordered marker, width 5. See the width-1 branch above for why the widths are spelled out one branch at a time.

The attribute-glued ordered marker (`1.{#x} item`, `.{#x} item`), on the minimum content column for the same reason the glued bullet branch is: a block width is not whitespace and cannot be counted. Ordered markers use a trailing `.` or `)` only. A parenthesized `(1)` / `(a)` form is NOT a marker in Carve (it is too easily confused with prose), so no leading `(`. The BARE DOT is a marker on its own (carve#472): `.` continues an ordered sequence, and is the only marker allowed to drop its value. The lookahead admits a marker glued to an attribute block (`.{#x}`, `3.{#k v}`), which is how the corpus writes it - but the ATTRIBUTE FORM NEEDS CONTENT TOO: `1.{#x}` with nothing after the block is a paragraph, so the glued-block branch spells the block out in full rather than skipping it. A `\{[^}]*\}` run stops in the wrong place, because a quoted value may contain `}` and may escape its own quote, and `{title="a}b"} x` is a valid item (markup-carve/carve-grammars#85). THE PAYLOAD MUST BE VALID, not merely brace-delimited: an invalid one means the `{` is literal content and the line is prose. `-{+a+} text` (corpus 90-list-item-attributes-6) and `1.{2=v} text` are paragraphs, while `-{} item` and `-{not attrs} item` are list items. Identifiers are STRICT (PART 9 S14) and admit no colon, which is what carve-js does (markup-carve/carve-grammars#126).

Definition-list TERM line: a leading `::` marker. Only the marker is scoped (mirroring the single-colon definition rule below), so a trailing `%% comment` and any inline markup in the term still tokenize normally. Matched before the single-colon rule; `::` never collides with a `:::+` fenced div, which needs three colons.
patterns.name: markup.list.definition.term.carve

patterns.comment: Definition-list DEFINITION line: a single `:` marker followed by the definition body.
patterns.name: markup.list.definition.carve

patterns.comment: A FOOTNOTE definition has a BODY, and that body's content column is a FIXED two whatever the label is wide, so it is the one definition shape that opens a container: `[^a]: note` over `  [r]: /u` collects the second definition (corpus a-definition-on-a-footnote-body-s-continuation-line-is-collected), one column in leaves it the document's own text, and three or more is the body's own text. Narrowing the definition rule below to flush-left without this would have dropped the scope from that shape entirely. A LINK reference definition gets no container, deliberately: it has no body at all, so an indented definition under one is a paragraph, not a second definition (measured against carve-php and carve-js - `[r]: /u` over `  [s]: /v` renders the second line as prose). `begin` consumes exactly what the definition rule below consumes and carries the same captures, so a footnote definition line tokenizes as it always did. Capture 0 carries the old rule-level `name`, which a begin/end rule cannot carry itself - a rule-level name spans the whole REGION, so the body lines would be scoped as definition too. A capture-0 name does NOT reach a sibling capture that re-tokenizes with its own patterns (vscode-textmate builds that sub-tokenization from the RULE stack, not from the capture's local stack), so the attribute capture names the scope itself or a trailing `{...}` block silently loses its definition layer. The trailing group captures an optional `{...}` attribute block using the same strict-identifier body #attributes validates, and recurses into #attributes so the block gets meta.link.reference.definition.carve (this rule's own name) layered with meta.attributes.carve and the entity captures - not only the sibling meta.attributes.carve it already got from the independent root #attributes pattern. Those attributes reach every link resolving the label (markup-carve/carve#612), so they are meaningful content, not decoration (markup-carve/vscode-carve#67).

FLUSH-LEFT: an indented definition at document level is prose, not a definition (corpus indented-reference-and-footnote-definitions-stay-literal). Indented spellings are reached through `#definitions-in-container`, which only a container's body can see, so the column question is answered by the container that opened rather than by this line on its own. The trailing group captures an optional `{...}` attribute block using the same strict-identifier body #attributes validates, and recurses into #attributes so the block gets meta.link.reference.definition.carve (this rule's own name) layered with meta.attributes.carve and the entity captures - not only the sibling meta.attributes.carve it already got from the independent root #attributes pattern. Those attributes reach every link resolving the label (markup-carve/carve#612), so they are meaningful content, not decoration (markup-carve/vscode-carve#67).
patterns.name: meta.link.reference.definition.carve

patterns.comment: An abbreviation definition is recognized only at document level (markup-carve/carve#611), unlike a link/footnote reference definition, which a container also collects. So this pattern is anchored at literal column 0 - no leading whitespace - while the reference-definition pattern above stays column-agnostic. Indenting `*[HTML]: ...` inside a list item, block quote, or any other container makes it inert prose, not a definition (markup-carve/vscode-carve#65).
patterns.name: meta.abbreviation.definition.carve

patterns.comment: A quoted title may contain escaped characters (`"ti\"tle"`), so the title run must consume `\\.` pairs instead of stopping at the first backslash - otherwise the whole link loses its scoping.
patterns.name: meta.link.inline.carve
meta.span.inline.carve
patterns.comment: THE BRACE RUN HAS TO BE A REAL ATTRIBUTE BLOCK. The lookahead was `(?={)`, which asked only that a brace follow - so `[a]{xlink:href=u}` scoped as a span while every engine renders the whole line as literal text, because an attribute name admits no colon (spec markup-carve/carve#870, corpus `an-attribute-name-admits-no-colon`). It now looks ahead for the same block the `attributes` rule matches, including the empty `{}` form that is valid only glued to a preceding `]`.
Same escaped-title handling as the inline link: consume `\\.` pairs inside the quoted title.
patterns.name: meta.image.inline.carve

patterns.comment: Inline footnote `^[content]` (core Carve). Its content is inline-parsed (spec `inline_footnote = '^[', inline_content, ']'`), so nested emphasis and code still tokenize. The `(?=$)` alternative in `end` bounds the span to one line so an unclosed `^[` cannot leak into following paragraphs. The `(?![ \t]*\])` guard keeps the opener from firing on an EMPTY note: `inline_content` is not optional, so `x ^[]` and `x ^[ ]` are literal text and `x ^[]{.c}` is a literal caret followed by a SPAN, yet all three used to highlight as a footnote (corpus an-empty-inline-note-is-literal).
patterns.name: meta.footnote.inline.carve

patterns.comment: Consume a backslash escape before the `end` check so `^[a \] b]` does not terminate at the escaped bracket.
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.carve

citations.comment: Citation group: a bracket whose content contains at least one @key and has no (url)/[ref]/{attrs} tail. A leading + signals an integral/in-text citation. Items are ;-separated; each may carry a -/+ prefix and an optional , locator. The @key and the -/+ per-item markers are scoped distinctly, analogous to @mention but inside the citation bracket.

patterns.name: markup.citation.carve
patterns.comment: Match the whole citation bracket [+?...@key...]  that is NOT followed by (, [, or { (which would make it a link, ref-link, or span). A lookahead for @ inside the brackets discriminates from plain spans and footnote refs.
Optional -/+ per-item modifier immediately before the @key
patterns.name: keyword.operator.citation.modifier.carve

patterns.comment: @key: citation key with allowed charset [A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_:.#$%&+?<>~/-]*
patterns.name: variable.other.citation.key.carve

patterns.comment: Semicolon item separator
patterns.name: punctuation.separator.citation.carve

code-callouts.comment: CodeCallout markers: <N> where N is one or more digits. Leading form at the start of a callout annotation line (^<N> prose); trailing form inside fenced-code body lines (code  <N>). Both share the same scope.

patterns.comment: Leading callout annotation line: <N> at the very start (with optional leading whitespace), followed by a space and annotation prose.
patterns.name: markup.callout.annotation.carve

patterns.comment: Trailing callout marker inside a code line: <N> at the end of the line (optionally preceded by whitespace).
patterns.name: markup.callout.marker.carve

patterns.comment: An empty attribute block is valid only glued to a preceding `]` (`[x]{}` -> x, corpus 66); a bare `{}` in prose is literal text (corpus 123).
patterns.name: meta.attributes.carve

patterns.comment: Strict identifier (spec PART 9 S14): a class/id/key may not start with a digit, so `{2=v}` stays literal text instead of scoping as an attribute block. An unquoted value may contain dots and colons (`{k=v.w}`); a quoted value may contain an escaped quote (`{title="a\"b"}`); a bare `{}` stays literal.
patterns.name: meta.attributes.carve
entity.other.attribute-name.carve
patterns.comment: No colon. The enclosing match already forbids one, so this could never paint a colon-bearing name and the two only disagreed on paper - but a reader checking the rule found the permissive spelling first (spec markup-carve/carve#870).

An unquoted value may contain dots and colons (k=v.w); consume it whole so the dot is not mistaken for a class. The lookbehind carries the KEY as well as the `=`, because a sub-pattern's lookbehind reads the whole line and not just the captured attribute block: a bare `(?<==)` also fired on an `=` sitting immediately BEFORE the opening brace, so a table cell whose attributes follow the header-kind marker (`|={.total}`) matched `{.total` as one unquoted value and lost the class scope. `|{.total}`, `|>{.num}` and `|=<{.h}` all scoped correctly, which is why it read as a table defect rather than an attribute one. A key always ends in an identifier character, so requiring one cannot exclude a real `key=value`.
patterns.name: string.unquoted.attribute.carve

patterns.comment: Closed span, like #inline-code: a match rule is line-bounded, so an unclosed opener cannot leak literal scoping into the rest of the document.
patterns.name: markup.raw.inline.literal.carve

patterns.comment: Closed span, like #inline-code: a match rule is line-bounded, so an unclosed opener cannot leak math scoping into the rest of the document. Display ($$) is tried before inline ($).
patterns.name: markup.other.math.display.carve

forced-emphasis.comment: Forced intraword emphasis (spec PART 9 S22): `{*x*}`, `{/x/}`, `{_x_}`, `{~x~}`. Content runs to the closing delimiter, so it may contain the delimiter itself (`{/a/b/}` -> a/b, corpus 01-emphasis-13). These MUST be listed before `#attributes`, because a forced span like `{_path_}` (corpus 01-emphasis-12) is shape-identical to a boolean attribute block and would otherwise be mis-scoped as one.

patterns.comment: A COMMENT FENCE MAY OPEN ON A BLOCK-QUOTE MARKER LINE (`> %%%`) too, and the same rule hides its body: spec PART 9 section 24 S2 with section 28 make a comment's body verbatim and invisible WHEREVER the fence sits (corpus 70-blocks-that-render-to-nothing - `> q` / `> %%%` / `> x` / `> %%%` / `> body` renders the quote with `q` and `body` only, markup-carve/vscode-carve#115). tree-sitter-carve is the reference: it puts a fenced_comment_block INSIDE the quote's content, beside the block_quote_marker rather than over it, with the body as a single opaque content node. This grammar INVERTED it - the `%%%` fell through to #trailing-comment and scoped as a LINE comment so no block opened, and the hidden `[r]: /url` came back as a live meta.link.reference.definition.carve on the line below, which is the same failure #113 fixed one marker over. Reached from #block-quotes rather than from #container-body, and NOT by including #comment-fence-on-marker-line: the begin is identical but the end cannot be shared. That rule's closer is INDENTED (`^[ \\t]+`) and its boundary is a column-0 line, and inside a quote both are backwards - the closer carries a `>` marker at column 0 and a column-0 `>` line is the CONTINUATION, not the boundary. Included as-is it closes zero-width on the very next line and hides only the opener. Anchored on \\G for the reason markup-carve/vscode-carve#67 gives for the in-quote reference definition beside it: the quote's own begin has already consumed `> `, so ^ can never match again on that line, and vscode-textmate resets \\G on every following line so this can never open one. The `(?<=[ \\t])` guard keeps it to the marker line - a later match on the same line moves the anchor too, and a percent run glued to the end of one (`> /a/%%%`) is not a fence. Capture 1 is the run of FURTHER markers, so a fence opened at `> > ` is closed at `> > ` and not at `> `; capture 2 is the fence, repeated in the closer so the width matches exactly and `%%%%` does not close `%%%`. The end's second branch is a zero-width quote boundary: an UNMARKED line is where the quote can end, and the engine degrades an unclosed opener to a line comment rather than hiding anything (`> %%%` / `> c` / blank line leaves `c` VISIBLE). Without it an unclosed opener would run to end of document.
patterns.name: comment.block.carve

patterns.comment: A COMMENT FENCE MAY OPEN ON A LIST ITEM'S MARKER LINE (`- %%%`), and then its body is hidden exactly as it is anywhere else: spec PART 9 section 24 S2 with section 28 make a comment's body verbatim and invisible WHEREVER the fence sits, so the whole run from opener to closer is one comment and nothing after it is affected (corpus 337-a-comment-fence-opened-on-an-item-s-marker-line-hides-its-body-too, markup-carve/vscode-carve#113). The `#comments` fence cannot reach that shape: its begin is anchored on ^, and the container's own begin match has already consumed `- ` by the time this line is scanned. The result was INVERTED highlighting - the `%%%` fell through to the trailing-comment rule and scoped as a LINE comment so no block opened, the hidden `[r]: /url` came back as a live meta.link.reference.definition.carve, and the REAL closer was then taken for an opener and swallowed the paragraph below. tree-sitter-carve is the reference here (all three carve-grammars highlighters were wrong, each differently): it puts a fenced_comment_block INSIDE list_item_content, beside the list_marker_* rather than over it, with the body as a single opaque content node. Anchored on \G rather than ^ for the reason markup-carve/vscode-carve#67 gives for the in-quote reference definition - \G matches at the current scan position, which on a marker line is exactly where the marker ended, and which vscode-textmate resets on every following line so this can never open one. The `(?<=[ \t])` guard is what keeps it to a marker line specifically: a later match on the same line moves the \G anchor too, and a `%%%` run glued to the end of one (`- /a/%%%`) is not a fence. The end has TWO branches. The first is the ordinary closer, INDENTED because the closer sits at the item's content column. The second is a zero-width container boundary: a column-0 line ends the item and with it the open fence, so corpus 326-a-column-0-line-after-a-container-s-last-block-when-that-block-left-no-paragraph-open-6 (`- %%%` / `c` / `%%%` / `tail`) keeps `c` and `tail` VISIBLE with the unclosed opener degrading to a line comment. Without it an unclosed opener would run to end of document, which is the failure this rule exists to remove.
patterns.name: comment.block.carve

container-body.comment: The pattern set a container's body reaches, shared by every rule that opens one so they cannot drift apart. It is the top-level list minus `#frontmatter`, which is document-start only, with `#definitions-in-container` standing in for `#definitions`: a definition is flush-left at document level and indented here, and the container's `end` has already established that an indented line inside it sits at or beyond the container's content column. `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` leads, and is reachable ONLY from here: it is the one rule that has to fire mid-line, on the container's own opening line.

definitions-in-container.comment: The indented spelling of a link or footnote reference definition, reachable only from a container's body. The container's `end` has already established that the line sits at or beyond that container's content column, which is the part a line-anchored `^[ \t]*` cannot know on its own. The trailing group captures an optional `{...}` attribute block using the same strict-identifier body #attributes validates, and recurses into #attributes so the block gets meta.link.reference.definition.carve (this rule's own name) layered with meta.attributes.carve and the entity captures - not only the sibling meta.attributes.carve it already got from the independent root #attributes pattern. Those attributes reach every link resolving the label (markup-carve/carve#612), so they are meaningful content, not decoration (markup-carve/vscode-carve#67).

hard-break.comment: A trailing backslash is a HARD BREAK, and it survives into the rendered line - the line block cases keep it (corpus a-line-block-s-hard-break-keeps-its-backslash and a-line-block-s-last-body-line-keeps-its-backslash). carve-grammars and the intellij-carve bundle have both scoped it as constant.character.escape.hard-break.carve since before this port; this grammar had no rule for it at all, so the backslash tokenized as ordinary text. Same match and same scope as those two on purpose: a third spelling of one production is how the three grammars drift.

block-quote-body.comment: The pattern set a block quote's own line reaches, shared by `#block-quotes` and `#block-quote-on-marker-line` so the two cannot drift apart - the same reason `#container-body` exists for containers. Both rules differ only in their anchor: one opens at the line start, the other at the scan position on a list item's marker line.

patterns.comment: A link/footnote reference definition is collected wherever its container puts it (markup-carve/carve#660), so it is recognized inside a quote too - unlike an abbreviation definition, which stays document-level-only (markup-carve/carve#611) and is deliberately NOT duplicated here. Anchored on \G rather than ^: the quote's own begin match has already consumed the `> ` prefix, so ^ (true column 0 of the line) can never match again on the same line - \G matches at the current scan position instead (markup-carve/vscode-carve#67).
patterns.name: meta.link.reference.definition.carve

patterns.comment:
A BLOCK QUOTE MAY OPEN ON A LIST ITEM'S OWN MARKER LINE (`- > x`, `1. > x`, `- - > x`, `- [ ] > x`), and it takes the rest of that line: carve-js at the pinned engine renders `

  • x

`. `#block-quotes` cannot reach it - its begin is anchored on ^, and the container's own begin match has already consumed the marker by the time this line is scanned - so the whole line fell through to the list rule and everything after the marker carried NO scope at all, while `- > %%%` inverted the same way `#113` and `#115` describe: the `%%%` scoped as a trailing LINE comment so no block opened, and the hidden `[r]: /url` came back live (markup-carve/vscode-carve#125). Anchored on \G with the `(?<=[ \t])` guard for the reasons `#comment-fence-on-marker-line` gives: \G matches at the current scan position, which on a marker line is where the marker ended, vscode-textmate resets it on every following line so this can never open one, and the guard keeps it to a marker line rather than to a `>` glued after some earlier match. Reachable ONLY from `#container-body`, so a document-level line can never take it. The marker keeps its own quote punctuation scope, which is tree-sitter-carve's split (markup-carve/tree-sitter-carve#218): the `block_quote` sits inside `list_item_content` beside the `list_marker_*` rather than over it.
patterns.name: markup.quote.carve
